facts.claim: Bonnie Bloomgarden is credited as the writer and composer of "Pink Radiation".
"Pink Radiation" is track 5 on Death Valley Girls' album Glow in the Dark, released June 10, 2016, and runs about five minutes.
Glow in the Dark first came out in 2016 on Burger Records (BRGR933). Suicide Squeeze Records reissued it on vinyl in 2021 (SSQ180).

The album was recorded at Station House Studio by Mark Rains. Only one song, "Death Valley Boogie", was recorded elsewhere (Valley Recording Co., by Joe Cardamone), so "Pink Radiation" was a Station House session.
Bonnie Bloomgarden said the album was recorded over two days with engineer Mark Rains at Station House Studio in Echo Park, California. She described the experience as kind of cosmic.
Album credits list Alana Amram, Bonnie Bloomgarden, Jessie Jones, Larry Schemel and Laura Kelsey as performers. Jim Kissling mastered the record.

The band said they made the songs to introduce rock & roll to the dead, then chose to introduce it to the living. Glow in the Dark was recorded as a call to arms for other concepts they were working on.
Glow in the Dark was the band's second full-length. It documented lineup changes: Alana Amram replaced Rachel Orosco on bass, and Jessie Jones joined to share vocals with Bloomgarden.
Death Valley Girls are a Los Angeles rock band formed in 2013. Their later albums Darkness Rains (2018), Under the Spell of Joy (2020) and Islands in the Sky (2023) came out on Suicide Squeeze.
The band shot a video for "Disco" from this album with Kansas, who later made the video for "Disaster (Is What We're After)" from Darkness Rains.

research.lineage: Death Valley Girls sit in the Los Angeles garage and punk rock underground, tied to Burger Records and later Suicide Squeeze, and one interviewer described them as a proto-punk, rock 'n' roll gang.

draft:
**Pink Radiation** is built on a held chord. A distorted electric guitar sustains it while a second guitar picks out a melodic line on top, the bass stays on root notes, and the drums push a medium-fast beat with the snare sitting right at the front. Over that, one voice sings high and sustained, raw at the edges, with no harmony to soften it. The reverb on the voice and guitars makes the room feel larger than a garage, but the grit stays. The parts lock into a pattern and hold it, and that steadiness is where the song gets its pull.

There's a reason it sounds like a summons. Death Valley Girls have said they made these songs to introduce rock & roll to the dead, then decided to introduce it to the living instead, and that **Glow in the Dark** was recorded as a call to arms. That's a joke and a mission statement at once, and this track takes the mission part seriously. The single unharmonized voice, stretched over a beat that won't let up, sounds less like a performance and more like calling out across a long distance and expecting to be heard.

The circumstances help. Bonnie Bloomgarden, credited as the song's writer, said the album was cut over two days with engineer Mark Rains at Station House Studio in Echo Park, and described the experience as kind of cosmic. You can hear the two-day speed in how little the track is fussed over. Nothing is polished down, and the thick, gritty texture sounds like a band playing in one room rather than a stack of overdubs. Glow in the Dark was the band's second full-length and documented a changing lineup, with Alana Amram arriving on bass and Jessie Jones joining to share vocals with Bloomgarden. The credits also list Larry Schemel and Laura Kelsey.

The record first came out on Burger Records, the label at the center of the Los Angeles garage underground, and one interviewer called the band a proto-punk, rock 'n' roll gang. That fits. This is the proto-punk idea that a few chords and a fixed beat, repeated with total conviction, can carry more feeling than a clever arrangement. At five minutes, the song gives that repetition room to build into a kind of trance instead of a quick blast.

What makes it stick is the devotion: one voice and a riff that won't quit, believing hard enough that you end up believing with them.
